original_question: Determine whether sporadic Costas arrays form only a finite set, or whether they instead arise from one or more still-unknown generally applicable construction techniques.
target_in_paper: Section 4.3 ("Sporadic Costas arrays"), Problem 5: "Settle the status of sporadic Costas arrays: are they finitely many? Are there new generally applicable construction techniques that produce them?" ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1102.5727))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the exact object of study (sporadic Costas arrays) and the exact status question posed in the paper: whether there are only finitely many such arrays, versus whether they are manifestations of still-unknown generally applicable construction techniques. That is very close to the paper's official wording and intent. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1102.5727))
missing_details: The draft does not define a Costas array/permutation. In the paper, a Costas permutation is a bijection f:[n]->[n] whose distance vectors (f(i)-f(j), i-j) are all distinct; the corresponding Costas array is the associated n x n permutation array. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1102.5727))
The draft does not define "sporadic". In Section 3.2.3, a Costas array is sporadic iff it is neither generated nor emergent. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1102.5727))

To make "generated" stand alone, the paper defines a generated family as an infinite family constructed by an algorithm whose applicability is determined by a sufficient condition involving only the order n of the array. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1102.5727))

To make "emergent" stand alone, the paper splits it into predictably emergent and unpredictably emergent families, both obtained by transformations of generated Costas arrays; the former are certified by a condition involving the order and additional parameters, while the latter require direct verification of the Costas property. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1102.5727))

The paper's Problem 5 is phrased as two status questions, not as a strict exclusive alternative: "are they finitely many?" and "are there new generally applicable construction techniques that produce them?" A fully paper-faithful rewrite should preserve that structure. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1102.5727))

The quantification is over finite Costas arrays of arbitrary order n. There is no ambient ring/field, no homogeneity or degree restriction, no nilpotency condition, no operator definition beyond the Costas-permutation formulation, and no "for all sufficiently large m" clause. The hidden parameters that matter here are the order n and the generated/emergent/sporadic classification. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1102.5727))

Problem 5 speaks about sporadic Costas arrays themselves, not explicitly about equivalence classes (ECs). Your phrase "finite set" is mathematically fine, but the stand-alone question should avoid drifting into an EC-counting variant. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1102.5727))
refined_question: Let [n]={1,...,n}. A Costas array of order n is an n x n permutation array, equivalently a bijection f:[n]->[n], such that all displacement vectors between pairs of dots are distinct. Call an infinite family of Costas arrays generated if it is produced by an algorithm whose applicability is determined by a sufficient condition involving only n, and call an infinite family emergent if it is obtained from generated Costas arrays by transformation, either under a condition involving n and additional parameters or only by direct verification of the Costas property. A Costas array is sporadic if it belongs to neither a generated family nor an emergent family. Settle the status of sporadic Costas arrays: are there only finitely many sporadic Costas arrays, and are there new generally applicable construction techniques that produce them? ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1102.5727))
justification: This draft is targeting Section 4.3, Problem 5 specifically, not the later questions on the scope of dot-addition methods, failed alternative constructions, or stochastic search in Section 5, because it asks about the global status of sporadic Costas arrays themselves and mirrors the exact dichotomy stated immediately before Problem 5: sporadic arrays may eventually disappear, leaving only finitely many, or they may be instances of unknown generally applicable construction techniques. The only additions needed to make the question truly stand alone are the paper's definitions of Costas array, generated family, emergent family, and sporadic array. ([ar5iv.org](https://ar5iv.org/pdf/1102.5727))
